nodes.title: 研究问题与背景
nodes.summary: 本研究旨在衡量生成式 AI 在真实工作场所的经济影响，重点关注生产力、技能偏向及组织结果。研究基于 5,179 名客服代理的数据，发现 AI 工具平均提升生产力 14%，且主要惠及新手和低技能员工。
paragraphs: 生成式人工智能（Generative AI）的出现引起了广泛关注，但关于其经济影响的实地研究甚少。尽管实验室环境表现良好，但其“幻觉”风险引发了对实际部署效果的担忧。
本文研究了生成式 AI 对话助手在一家财富 500 强软件公司的客户服务部门的部署情况。这是已知的首个关于生成式 AI 在工作场所大规模部署影响的研究。
研究利用 5,179 名客服代理的数据，发现访问 AI 助手使代理的生产力（以每小时解决的问题数量衡量）平均提高了 14%。这种增长主要体现在经验不足和低技能工人身上，而对经验丰富和高技能工人的影响微乎其微。
作者提出，这种现象发生是因为机器学习系统捕捉并传播了高能力工人的行为模式（即隐性知识），帮助新工人更快地沿着经验曲线移动。此外，AI 辅助还改善了客户情绪，减少了对管理层干预的请求，并提高了员工保留率。

claims.statement: 访问 AI 助手使客服代理的生产力（每小时解决的问题数）平均提高了 14%。
conditions: 基于 5,179 名代理的实地数据
主要惠及新手和低技能工人

claims.statement: AI 带来的生产力提升不成比例地惠及经验较少和技能较低的工人，对高技能工人影响最小。
conditions: 与以往计算机化浪潮的技能偏向技术变革不同

claims.statement: AI 辅助改善了客户情绪，减少了寻求管理层干预的请求，并提高了员工保留率。
conditions: 作为组织结果的额外发现

assumptions: 研究假设 AI 工具主要作为辅助工具，而非完全替代人工。
假设观察到的相关性在控制固定效应后能反映因果影响（需结合实证策略部分验证）。

nodes.title: AI 系统机制与隐性知识传播
nodes.summary: 该 AI 系统基于 GPT 系列大型语言模型，经过特定客服对话数据的微调。它通过实时监控聊天并提供实时建议来增强代理能力。核心假设是系统捕捉了高技能代理的隐性知识模式，并将其传递给低技能代理。
paragraphs: 研究的 AI 工具建立在 OpenAI 开发的 GPT 系列大型语言模型的最新版本之上。该系统监控客户聊天，并为代理提供如何响应的实时建议。
系统设计为增强（augment）而非替代代理。代理对对话负责，可以自由忽略建议。输出仅显示给代理，由代理决定是否采纳。
系统使用大量标记的客户 - 代理对话数据进行训练，标记包括通话是否成功解决、处理时间以及代理是否为“顶级”绩效者。模型寻找最能预测通话解决和处理时间的对话模式。
进一步的训练类似于人类反馈强化学习（RLHF），优先选择表达同理心、提供适当技术文档链接并限制不专业语言的回复。
机制假设：由于模型是在人类生成的数据上训练的，且个体代理能力存在差异，模型在识别成功与不成功通话的模式时，隐式地学习了高技能与低技能工人的特征差异。因此，AI 建议可以被视为编码了高技能工人的对话模式并将其传播给其他工人。

claims.statement: AI 系统设计为增强人工代理，代理拥有是否采纳建议的完全决定权。
conditions: 输出仅对代理可见
代理可忽略建议

claims.statement: 模型使用标记有结果（如解决状态、处理时间）和代理绩效等级的大量历史对话数据进行训练。
conditions: 数据包含顶级绩效者的行为模式

claims.statement: AI 系统通过编码高技能工人的对话模式，将隐性知识传播给其他工人。
conditions: 高技能工人未因贡献这些模式而获得额外补偿
低技能工人通过遵循建议模仿高技能行为

steps.title: 步骤 1: 实时监控与输入
steps.text: 系统实时监控客户与代理之间的聊天内容，获取对话历史和当前上下文。

steps.title: 步骤 2: 模式匹配与建议生成
steps.text: 基于训练数据中学到的模式（特别是高绩效代理的行为），系统生成两种主要输出：1) 如何回复客户的实时建议；2) 相关技术问题的内部文档链接。

steps.title: 步骤 3: 人工决策与执行
steps.text: 建议仅显示给代理。代理全权决定是否完全或部分采纳建议，或者在系统因数据不足未提供建议时自行回复。这减少了错误或不相关内容进入客户对话的风险。

assumptions: 假设历史数据中高绩效代理的行为模式确实是导致成功的关键因素。
假设代理在大多数情况下会理性地评估并采纳有益的建议。
系统在缺乏足够训练数据的情况下不会提供建议（这在少数情况下发生）。

nodes.title: 实证策略与识别方法
nodes.summary: 研究采用交错部署（staggered deployment）设计，利用双重差分（Difference-in-Differences）模型识别 AI 访问的因果影响。为解决异质性处理效应带来的偏差，主要使用 Sun & Abraham (2021) 提出的交互加权估计量。
paragraphs: AI 助手在代理层面逐步 rollout，大部分采用发生在 2020 年 11 月至 2021 年 2 月之间。这种交错的部署时间为因果推断提供了变异来源。
基准回归模型为：y_it = δ_t + α_i + β*AI_it + γ*X_it + ε_it。其中 y_it 是结果变量（如每小时解决数），AI_it 是代理 i 在时间 t 是否访问 AI 的指示变量。模型包含时间固定效应（δ_t）和代理固定效应（α_i）。
由于处理效应可能随时间变化或因采用队列不同而异（例如，后期采用的代理可能适应更快），传统的两向固定效应（TWFE）回归可能产生偏差。
因此，研究首选使用 Sun & Abraham (2021) 提出的交互加权（IW）估计量来分析处理效应的动态变化。该估计量在平行趋势和无预期行为假设下是一致的。
主要生产力指标是每小时解决数（RPH），由平均处理时间、每小时聊天数和解决率共同决定。数据显示，处理后代理的平均处理时间从 40 分钟降至 35 分钟，RPH 显著提升。

claims.statement: 研究利用 AI 工具在代理层面的交错部署，采用双重差分模型识别因果影响。
conditions: 控制时间和代理固定效应
大部分部署发生在 2020 年 11 月至 2021 年 2 月

claims.statement: 为处理异质性处理效应，研究首选 Sun & Abraham (2021) 的交互加权估计量，而非传统的两向固定效应模型。
conditions: 传统 TWFE 在处理效应随时间或队列变化时可能有偏
假设满足平行趋势和无预期行为

claims.statement: 主要结果指标为每小时解决数（RPH），处理后代理的 RPH 增加了约 13.8%（0.30 次通话）。
conditions: 控制代理固定效应和任期后
平均处理时间显著下降

assumptions: 平行趋势假设：在没有 AI 干预的情况下，处理组和对照组的结果变化趋势相同。
无预期行为：代理在正式获得 AI 访问权之前不会改变其行为。
队列特定的处理效应遵循相同的动态 profile（针对 Sun & Abraham 估计量）。

nodes.title: 主要结果：生产力提升
nodes.summary: 本研究的核心发现是，生成式 AI 辅助工具使客服代理每小时解决的对话数量平均增加了约 14%。这一增长主要源于两个机制：单次对话处理时间的缩短（减少约 9%）以及代理同时处理多个对话能力的提升。数据表明，AI 并未以牺牲解决率或客户满意度为代价来换取速度。
paragraphs: 根据表 2（Table 2）的回归分析，在控制了时间、地点、代理个体固定效应及任期变量后，AI 模型的部署使每小时解决量（Resolutions Per Hour, RPH）增加了 0.30 次对话，相对于基准均值 2.17 次，增幅为 13.8%（原文报告为 14% 左右）。若仅控制时间和地点固定效应而不控制代理个体差异，估算的增幅高达 22.2%，但在加入更严格的控制变量后，效应值趋于保守且稳定。

表 3（Table 3）进一步揭示了生产力提升的具体构成。首先，平均处理时长（Average Handle Time）减少了 3.8 分钟，降幅达 9%。其次，代理每小时能处理的对话数（Chats Per Hour）增加了 0.37 次，增幅约为 14%。作者指出，由于“每小时对话数”考虑了多任务处理能力，其效应强于单纯的处理时长缩短，说明 AI 不仅加快了单次回复速度，还增强了代理并行处理多个客户请求的能力。
关于质量指标，数据显示解决率（Resolution Rate）有小幅上升（1.3 个百分点，显著性水平 10%），而客户满意度（NPS）未出现具有经济意义的显著变化。这表明生产力的提升并非通过草率结束对话或降低服务质量实现。

claims.statement: AI 部署使每小时解决量（RPH）平均增加 13.8%（0.30 次对话）。
conditions: 控制代理个体固定效应和任期变量
基于表 2 第 3 列和第 6 列的回归结果

claims.statement: 生产力提升由处理时间缩短（-9%）和多任务处理能力增强共同驱动，后者效应更强。
conditions: 基于表 3 对平均处理时长和每小时对话数的对比分析

claims.statement: 生产力提升未导致客户满意度显著下降，解决率有小幅提升。
conditions: NPS 变化无经济显著性
解决率提升 1.3 个百分点

assumptions: 平行趋势假设（Parallel Trends）：在没有 AI 干预的情况下，处理组和对照组的生产力变化趋势应保持一致。
无预期行为（No Anticipatory Behavior）：代理在正式获得 AI 访问权之前不会提前改变工作行为。
回归模型控制了时间不变的个人特征和时间变化的任期因素，以隔离 AI 的因果效应。

nodes.title: 异质性分析：技能偏向型变革
nodes.summary: AI 带来的生产力增益在不同技能水平的代理间分布极不均匀。数据显示，低技能（新手）代理获益最大，每小时解决量提升高达 35%；而高技能（专家）代理几乎没有获得生产力提升，甚至在某些质量指标上出现轻微负面影响。这与传统 IT 技术往往更利于高技能工人的文献结论形成鲜明对比。
paragraphs: 作者根据 AI 部署前三个月的平均表现（处理时长、解决率、满意度）将代理分为五个技能五分位组（Quintiles）。图 6 Panel A 显示，处于最低技能五分位（Q1，最左侧）的代理，其每小时解决量提升了 35%。相比之下，最高技能五分位（Q5，最右侧）的代理在生产力上没有显示出统计学显著的增长。
这种技能偏向性在其他指标上也得到印证（图 7）。对于低技能代理，AI 显著缩短了处理时间并提高了每小时对话数。然而，对于高技能代理，虽然每小时对话数略有增加，但处理时长未见显著减少，且解决率和客户满意度出现了统计上显著但幅度较小的下降。
作者推测，对于已经高效工作的专家级代理，AI 的建议可能成为一种干扰（distraction），导致他们在追求速度时略微牺牲了质量，或者他们原本的表现已接近天花板，AI 无法提供额外的边际增益。这一发现暗示生成式 AI 可能具有‘拉平’技能差距的作用，而非扩大它。

claims.statement: 最低技能五分位（Q1）的代理在接入 AI 后，每小时解决量提升了 35%。
conditions: 基于图 6 Panel A 的事件研究估计
技能定义为部署前的综合绩效表现

claims.statement: 最高技能五分位（Q5）的代理在生产率（每小时解决量）上未观察到显著增益。
conditions: 对比 Q1 与 Q5 的系数估计
图 6 Panel A 右侧数据点接近零

claims.statement: 高技能代理在获得 AI 辅助后，解决率和客户满意度出现小幅但统计显著的下降。
conditions: 基于图 7 Panel C 和 Panel D 的分析
解释为潜在的干扰效应

assumptions: 技能五分位的划分仅基于历史数据，不受 AI 部署后的表现影响（避免反向因果）。
不同技能组别在 AI 部署前满足平行趋势假设。
高技能代理的质量下降确实是由 AI 干扰引起，而非其他同期发生的因素（尽管模型已控制多种固定效应）。

nodes.title: 机制证据：经验曲线加速
nodes.summary: AI 辅助工具显著改变了新代理的学习轨迹，使其能够更快地达到熟练工的生产力水平。数据显示，拥有 AI 辅助的新代理仅需 2 个月即可达到无 AI 代理需 6 个月以上才能达到的生产力水平（约每小时 2.5 次解决量）。这种‘经验曲线’的陡峭化表明 AI 在知识传递和技能培训方面发挥了替代或增强作用。
paragraphs: 图 9（Figure 9）描绘了不同队列代理的生产力随任期（Tenure）变化的曲线。从未获得 AI 访问权的代理（Never Treated）表现出典型的学习曲线：从入职时的约 2.0 次/小时开始，缓慢爬升，直到 8-10 个月后才达到约 2.5 次/小时的水平。
相比之下，从入职第一天起就拥有 AI 访问权的代理（Always Treated）生产力增长极为迅速。他们在第 2 个月就达到了 2.5 次/小时的水平，并在第 5 个月时突破 3.0 次/小时。这意味着 AI 将新员工达到特定生产力阈值所需的时间从半年以上压缩到了两个月。
此外，研究还观察了一组在入职 5 个月后才获得 AI 访问权的代理（Treated 5 mo.）。他们在前 5 个月的成长轨迹与‘从未 treated'组完全重合，但在获得 AI 访问的瞬间，其生产力曲线立即向上转折，迅速追赶并融合了‘始终 treated'组的路径。这有力地证明了生产力的跳跃是由 AI 接入直接引起的，而非特定队列的固有特征。
作者特别注明，此处避免使用‘学习曲线’（learning curve）一词，因为无法区分代理是真正‘学会’了技能，还是仅仅在机械地遵循 AI 的建议。因此，更准确的描述是 AI 帮助代理更快地沿经验曲线下移（move down the experience curve）。

claims.statement: 有 AI 辅助的新代理在 2 个月内达到的生产力水平，无 AI 代理需要 6 个月以上才能达到。
conditions: 目标生产力水平约为 2.5 次解决量/小时
基于图 9 中 Always Treated 与 Never Treated 曲线的对比

claims.statement: 在入职 5 个月后获得 AI 访问权的代理，其生产力曲线立即发生结构性断裂并快速上升。
conditions: 前 5 个月轨迹与无 AI 组一致
第 5 个月接入点后轨迹与始终有 AI 组趋同

steps.title: 阶段一：自然成长期 (0-5 个月)
steps.text: 所有新代理（无论未来是否获得 AI）在入职初期都遵循相同的缓慢成长轨迹。生产力从约 2.0 次/小时起步，依靠自然经验积累缓慢提升。此时，‘晚获得 AI 组’与‘从未获得 AI 组’的曲线完全重合。

steps.title: 阶段二：干预点 (第 5 个月)
steps.text: 对于‘晚获得 AI 组’，在第 5 个月发生结构性变化。一旦接入 AI 系统，其生产力曲线立即脱离原有的缓慢增长路径，出现明显的向上跳跃。

steps.title: 阶段三：加速追赶期 (5 个月后)
steps.text: 获得 AI 后，该组代理的生产力增长斜率变得极陡，迅速追平甚至超过那些从一开始就有 AI 辅助的资深代理。这证明生产力的飞跃是 AI 介入的直接结果，而非时间推移的自然产物。

assumptions: 不同入职队列的代理在潜在能力上没有系统性差异（即‘晚获得 AI 组’若不获得 AI，其轨迹会与‘从未获得 AI 组’保持一致）。
样本在 5 个月后截断，因为超过 5 个月的处理后观测值较少（见脚注 15），这可能限制了对长期效应的推断。
生产力的提升归因于 AI 建议的直接执行，而非代理通过 AI 学到了可迁移的隐性知识（作者明确区分了‘遵循建议’与‘学习’）。

nodes.title: 文本证据：沟通模式的趋同
nodes.summary: 本节通过文本嵌入分析证明，AI 辅助使低技能客服人员的语言风格向高技能人员靠拢。数据显示，低技能员工在使用 AI 后，其沟通内容与高技能员工的余弦相似度从 0.55 提升至 0.61，表明 AI 可能编码并传递了高绩效者的隐性知识（tacit knowledge）。
paragraphs: 为了探究 AI 如何影响工作表现，研究者对客服对话进行了文本分析。他们使用 all-MiniLM-L6-v2 模型生成文本嵌入，并计算余弦相似度来衡量语言风格的接近程度。分析聚焦于低技能（底部五分之一）和高技能（顶部五分之一）员工在 AI 部署前后的语言变化。
结果显示，低技能员工在获得 AI 辅助后，其语言模式发生了显著变化，变得更像高技能员工。具体而言，低技能与高技能员工之间的平均文本相似度从 0.55 上升至 0.61。虽然这一数值变化看似微小，但考虑到高技能员工自身的内部相似度仅为 0.73，这意味着语言差距得到了实质性缩小。
相比之下，高技能员工的语言风格在使用 AI 后变化较小，这符合预期，因为 AI 建议的往往是他们已经掌握的最佳实践。这种单向的趋同支持了 AI 作为隐性知识传递工具的假设，即它帮助经验不足的员工更快地习得专家的沟通策略，而不仅仅是加快打字速度。

claims.statement: AI 辅助导致低技能员工的语言风格向高技能员工趋同，两者间的文本相似度从 0.55 提升至 0.61。
conditions: 基于余弦相似度测量
控制代理任期和对话时间
仅针对获得 AI 访问权的低技能组

claims.statement: 低技能员工比高技能员工表现出更大的语言风格转变，支持 AI 传递隐性知识的假设。
conditions: 高技能定义为预部署生产力的前五分之一
低技能定义为后五分之一

assumptions: 文本嵌入模型 (all-MiniLM-L6-v2) 能有效捕捉沟通中的风格和语义细微差别。
语言风格的趋同直接反映了隐性知识的转移，而非单纯的模板化回复。
高技能和低技能的分类基于部署前的生产力指数，且在分析期间保持相对稳定以进行对比。

nodes.title: 组织结果：情感分析与留存率
nodes.summary: 除了生产力提升，AI 辅助还带来了显著的组织层面收益。客户情感得分平均提升 0.18 分（约半个标准差），且员工流失率显著下降，特别是对于入职不到 6 个月的新员工，流失概率降低了约 10 个百分点。此外，客户请求升级（找经理）的情况减少了近 25%。
paragraphs: 研究使用 SiEBERT 模型对对话进行情感分析。结果显示，AI 辅助显著改善了客户的情感体验，平均得分提升 0.18 分。这种改善在入职 3-6 个月的员工中最为明显。相比之下，客服人员自身的情感得分本来就很高（均值 0.89），因此提升空间有限，仅微增 0.02 分。
在员工留存方面，AI 辅助使当月离职的可能性平均降低了 8.6 个百分点。对于工作经验少于 6 个月的新员工，这一效应更强，流失率降低了约 10 个百分点。鉴于新员工基准流失率约为 25%，这是一个巨大的改善，表明 AI 可能减轻了新人的工作压力或提高了其胜任感。
工作流程也发生了变化。客户要求与经理交谈的请求减少了近 25%，且这种减少随时间持续扩大。这表明一线员工在 AI 帮助下更能独立解决复杂问题。横向转接（转给其他部门）的数量变化不显著，但文本分析显示这些转接更多是为了将客户匹配到更专业的部门，而非因无法处理而推诿。

claims.statement: AI 辅助使客户情感得分平均提升 0.18 分，相当于半个标准差。
conditions: 基于 SiEBERT 模型分析
控制代理固定效应和时间固定效应
效应在中等任期员工中最大

claims.statement: AI 辅助使新员工（<6 个月任期）的月流失率降低约 10 个百分点。
conditions: 基准流失率约为 25%
未包含代理固定效应（因离职只发生一次）
可能存在选择偏差（公司可能优先给留任概率高的员工配 AI）

claims.statement: 客户请求与经理交谈的频率下降了近 25%。
conditions: 通过文本分析识别“找经理”请求
效应随时间持久且增长

assumptions: 情感分析模型的评分能准确反映人类在客服场景下的真实感受。
流失率的降低主要归因于 AI 带来的压力减轻，而非公司同期其他留人政策的变化。
请求“找经理”的文本模式能准确代表实际的升级需求，且未被 AI 建议的话术所掩盖。
作者明确指出，由于缺乏代理固定效应，流失率的结果可能被高估（若公司倾向于给更可能留任的员工部署 AI）。

nodes.title: 依从性与实施动态
nodes.summary: 员工对 AI 建议的平均依从率为 38%，且依从度与生产力增益呈正相关：依从度最高的五分之一员工生产力提升近 25%，而最低组也有 10% 的提升。随着时间推移，所有技能水平的员工依从率均有所上升，最终趋于收敛。
paragraphs: 研究定义“依从”为员工点击复制 AI 建议或输入极其相似的内容。总体平均依从率为 38%（四分位距 23%-50%），这与 GitHub Copilot 等其他生成式 AI 工具的使用率相当。作者指出，不完全依从可能是理性的，因为 AI 有时会提供错误或无意义的建议。
依从度与回报之间存在强烈的正相关关系。将员工按首月依从率分为五组，依从度最低组的 productivity 提升了 10%，而最高组提升了近 25%。这种关联在处理时间和每小时通话量上最为显著。然而，作者谨慎地指出，这可能是由于依从行为本身带来了收益，也可能是高生产力员工本身就倾向于更多地使用工具（选择性偏差）。
依从行为随时间演变。资深员工（任期>1 年）最初依从率较低（30%），低于新员工（37%），但他们的依从率增长速度更快，使得两组在 5 个月后趋同。同样，高技能员工起初依从率较低，但也逐渐向低技能员工看齐。这表明随着员工认识到 AI 的价值，怀疑态度会逐渐消退，或者强烈排斥 AI 的员工可能已离职。

claims.statement: 员工对 AI 建议的平均依从率为 38%，且依从度越高，生产力增益越大（最高组 +25% vs 最低组 +10%）。
conditions: 依从定义为复制或输入相似内容
控制年份 - 月份和代理固定效应
相关性可能受选择性偏差影响

claims.statement: 资深员工和高技能员工起初依从率较低，但随时间推移迅速增加，最终与新员工/低技能员工趋同。
conditions: 观测期为部署后 5 个月
资深定义为任期超过 1 年

steps.title: 初始状态：差异化的依从
steps.text: 在 AI 部署初期，资深员工（>1 年经验）的依从率仅为 30%，而新员工（<3 个月）为 37%。高技能员工也表现出较低的初始依从意愿。

steps.title: 动态过程：学习与适应
steps.text: 随着时间推移（部署后 1-5 个月），所有群体的依从率都在上升。值得注意的是，资深员工的依从率增长速度更快，显示出更快的学习曲线或对工具价值的重新评估。

steps.title: 最终状态：趋同
steps.text: 在部署 5 个月后，不同任期和技能水平的员工群体在依从率上趋于一致。这可能意味着怀疑者被说服，或者极度排斥者已离职。

assumptions: 依从率的计算准确反映了员工对 AI 建议的实际采纳程度。
依从度与生产力的相关性部分源于因果关系，尽管存在选择性偏差的可能性。
样本在 5 个月后截断是因为缺乏更多观测数据，而非依从行为在此时停止变化。
GitHub Copilot 的研究数据可作为合理的基准进行比较。

nodes.title: 研究局限与适用范围条件
nodes.summary: 本文提供了生成式 AI 在真实工作场所影响的首个实证证据，但结果受限于特定的稳定产品环境。作者明确指出，本研究旨在评估微观层面的生产力与组织行为变化，而非宏观的就业或工资效应。此外，文章强调了在快速变化的环境中历史数据训练模型的局限性，并提出了关于高技能员工数据贡献补偿的未决问题。
paragraphs: 本文的研究背景建立在稳定的产品和一套固定的技术支持问题之上（pdf-ac0a4e183aa6f936-p23-b17）。作者指出，在这种相对静态的环境中，基于历史数据训练的 AI 推荐系统能有效体现高技能员工的最佳实践（pdf-ac0a4e183aa6f936-p23-b8）。然而，这一结论不能直接推广到所有公司或生产流程，特别是在产品或环境快速变化的领域，AI 建议的相对价值可能会有所不同（pdf-ac0a4e183aa6f936-p23-b18, pdf-ac0a4e183aa6f936-p23-b19）。

在研究范围上，作者明确声明本文并非设计用于揭示生成式 AI 工具对总体就业或工资的宏观影响（pdf-ac0a4e183aa6f936-p4-b0, pdf-ac0a4e183aa6f936-p4-b1）。研究结果未捕捉到对技能需求、工作设计、工资或客户需求的潜在长期影响（pdf-ac0a4e183aa6f936-p23-b20）。例如，更有效的技术支持可能会加速呼叫中心代理承担更复杂责任的趋势，从而增加总需求，即使代理的生产力提高了（pdf-ac0a4e183aa6f936-p23-b21, pdf-ac0a4e183aa6f936-p23-b22）。

最后，研究引发了一个关于补偿机制的重要问题：员工是否应因其向 AI 系统提供的数据而获得补偿（pdf-ac0a4e183aa6f936-p23-b26）。高技能员工在模型开发中扮演重要角色，但在提高自身生产力方面看到的直接收益较小（pdf-ac0a4e183aa6f936-p23-b27, pdf-ac0a4e183aa6f936-p23-b28）。鉴于生成式 AI 尚处于早期阶段，这些问题需要进一步审查（pdf-ac0a4e183aa6f936-p23-b29）。

claims.statement: 本研究不旨在揭示生成式 AI 对总体就业或工资的宏观影响。
conditions: 研究设计专注于微观工作场所实证
不包含宏观经济模型分析

claims.statement: 研究结果主要适用于具有相对稳定产品和固定技术支持问题的环境。
conditions: 产品更新频率低
技术问题类型固定
依赖历史数据训练模型

claims.statement: 高技能员工为 AI 模型开发提供关键数据，但自身生产力提升受益较小，引发补偿公平性问题。
conditions: AI 系统内化了高技能员工的隐性知识
高技能员工主要作为知识提供者而非主要受益者

assumptions: 研究环境中的产品和技术支持问题保持相对稳定（pdf-ac0a4e183aa6f936-p23-b17）。
AI 系统的推荐主要基于历史交互数据训练（pdf-ac0a4e183aa6f936-p23-b19）。
高技能员工的工作模式包含可被 AI 学习并转移给低技能员工的隐性知识（pdf-ac0a4e183aa6f936-p23-b8）。

                            Generative AI at Work˚





                       Erik Brynjolfsson           Danielle Li         Lindsey Raymond

                                                  Abstract


               We study the staggered introduction of a generative AI-based conversational assistant using[econ.GN]             data from 5,179 customer support agents. Access to the tool increases productivity, as measured
                 by issues resolved per hour, by 14 percent on average, with the greatest impact on novice and
                     low-skilled workers, and minimal impact on experienced and highly skilled workers. We provide
                    suggestive evidence that the AI model disseminates the potentially tacit knowledge of more able
                   workers and helps newer workers move down the experience curve. In addition, we show that
                AI assistance improves customer sentiment, reduces requests for managerial intervention, and
                  improves employee retention.


           JEL Classiﬁcations: D80, J24, M15, M51, O33

            Keywords: Generative AI, Large Language Models, Technology Adoption, Worker Productiv-

                 ity, Organizational Design.arXiv:2304.11771v1

                  of Economic Research (NBER)’s working paper series, #WP31161. We are grateful to Daron Acemoglu, David Autor, Amittai
               Axelrod, Eleanor Dillon, Zayd Enam, Luis Garicano, Alex Frankel, Sam Manning, Sendhil Mullainathan, Emma Pierson, Scott
                 Stern, Ashesh Rambachan, John Van Reenen, Raﬀaella Sadun, Kathryn Shaw, Christopher Stanton, Sebastian Thrun, and

                content is solely the responsibility of the authors and does not necessarily represent the oﬃcial views of Stanford University,
             MIT, or the NBER.

The emergence of generative artiﬁcial intelligence (AI) has attracted signiﬁcant attention, but

there have been few studies of its economic impact. While various generative AI tools have per-

formed well in laboratory settings, excitement about their potential has been tempered by concerns

that these tools are prone to “hallucination,” and may produce coherent sounding but inaccurate

information (Peng et al., 2023a; Roose, 2023).

   In this paper, we study the adoption of a generative AI tool that provides conversational guidance

for customer support agents.1 This is, to our knowledge, the ﬁrst study of the impact of generative

AI when deployed at scale in the workplace. We ﬁnd that access to AI assistance increases the

productivity of agents by 14 percent, as measured by the number of customer issues they are able to

resolve per hour. In contrast to studies of prior waves of computerization, we ﬁnd that these gains

accrue disproportionately to less-experienced and lower-skill workers.2 We argue that this occurs

because ML systems work by capturing and disseminating the patterns of behavior that characterize

the most productive agents.

   Computers and software have transformed the economy with their ability to perform certain

tasks with far more precision, speed, and consistency than humans. To be eﬀective, these systems

typically require explicit and detailed instructions for how to transform inputs into outputs: when

engineers write code to perform a task, they are codifying that task. Yet because many production

processes rely on tacit knowledge, these processes have so far deﬁed automation (Polanyi, 1966;

Autor, 2014).

   Machine learning algorithms work diﬀerently.  In contrast to traditional programming, these

systems implicitly infer instructions from examples. Given a training set of images, for instance,

ML systems can learn to recognize faces. This highlights a key, distinguishing aspect of ML systems:

they can learn to perform tasks even when no instructions exist–including tasks requiring tacit

knowledge that could previously only be gained through lived experience (Polanyi, 1966; Autor,

2014; Brynjolfsson and Mitchell, 2017).3

  We study the impact of generative AI on productivity in the customer service sector, an indus-

try with one of the highest rates of AI adoption (Chui et al., 2021). We examine the staggered

  1A note on terminology. There are many deﬁnitions of artiﬁcial intelligence and of intelligence itself— Legg et
al. (2007) list over 70 of them. In this paper, we deﬁne “artiﬁcial intelligence” (AI) as an umbrella term that refers
to a computer system that is able to sense, reason, or act like a human. “Machine learning” (ML) is a branch of AI
that uses algorithms to learn from data, identify patterns and make predictions or decisions without being explicitly
programmed (Google, n.d.). Large language models (LLMs) and tools built around LLMs such as ChatGPT are
an increasingly important application of machine learning. LLMs generate new content, making them a form of
“generative AI.”
  2We provide a discussion of this literature at the end of this section.
   3As Meijer (2018) puts it “where the Software 1.0 Engineer formally speciﬁes their problem, carefully designs algo-
rithms, composes systems out of subsystems or decomposes complex systems into smaller components, the Software
2.0 Engineer amasses training data and simply feeds it into an ML algorithm...”



                                           1

deployment of a chat assistant using data from 5,000 agents working for a Fortune 500 software

ﬁrm that provides business process software. The tool we study is built on a recent version of the

Generative Pre-trained Transformer (GPT) family of large language models developed by OpenAI

(OpenAI, 2023). It monitors customer chats and provides agents with real-time suggestions for how

to respond. It is designed to augment agents, who remain responsible for the conversation and are

free to ignore its suggestions.

  We have four sets of ﬁndings.

    First, AI assistance increases worker productivity, resulting in a 13.8 percent increase in the

number of chats that an agent is able to successfully resolve per hour. This increase reﬂects shifts in

three components of productivity: a decline in the time it takes to an agent to handle an individual

chat, an increase in the number of chats that an agent is able to handle per hour (agents may handle

multiple calls at once), and a small increase in the share of chats that are successfully resolved.

   Second, AI assistance disproportionately increases the performance less skilled and less experi-

enced workers across all productivity measures we consider. In addition, we ﬁnd that the AI tool

helps newer agents move more quickly down the experience curve: treated agents with two months

of tenure perform just as well as untreated agents with over six months of tenure. These results

contrast, in spirit, with studies that ﬁnd evidence of skill-biased technical change for earlier waves

of computer technology (Autor et al., 2003; Acemoglu and Restrepo, 2018; Bresnahan et al., 2002;

Bartel et al., 2007).

   Our third set of results investigates the mechanism underlying our ﬁndings so far. We posit that

high-skill workers may have less to gain from AI assistance precisely because AI recommendations

capture the potentially tacit knowledge embodied in their own behaviors. Rather, low-skill workers

are more likely to improve by incorporating these behaviors by adhering to AI suggestions. Consis-

tent with this, we ﬁnd few positive eﬀects of AI access for the highest-skilled or most-experienced

workers. Instead, using textual analysis, we ﬁnd suggestive evidence that AI assistance leads lower-

skill agents to communicate more like high-skill agents.

    Finally, we show that the introduction of AI systems can impact the experience and organization

of work. We show that AI assistance markedly improves how customers treat agents, as measured

by the sentiments of their chat messages. This change may be associated with other organizational

changes: turnover decreases, particularly for newer workers, and customers are less likely to escalate

a call by asking to speak to an agent’s supervisor.

   Our overall ﬁndings demonstrate that generative AI working alongside humans can have a sig-

niﬁcant positive impact on the productivity and retention of individual workers. We emphasize,




                                           2

however, that our paper is not designed to shed light on the aggregate employment or wage eﬀects

of generative AI tools.

   Our paper is related to a large literature on the impact of various forms of technological adoption

on worker productivity and the organization of work (e.g. Rosen, 1981; Autor et al., 1998; Athey

and Stern, 2002; Bresnahan et al., 2002; Bartel et al., 2007; Acemoglu et al., 2007; Hoﬀman et al.,

2017; Bloom et al., 2014; Michaels et al., 2014; Garicano and Rossi-Hansberg, 2015; Acemoglu and

Restrepo, 2020). Many of these studies, particularly those focused on information technologies, ﬁnd

evidence that IT complements higher-skill workers (Akerman et al., 2015; Taniguchi and Yamada,

2022).  Bartel et al. (2007) shows that ﬁrms that adopt IT tend to use more skilled labor and

increase skill requirements for their workers. Acemoglu and Restrepo (2020) study the diﬀusion of

robots and ﬁnd that the negative employment eﬀects of robots are most pronounced for workers

in blue-collar occupations and those with less than a college education.  In contrast, we study a

diﬀerent type of technology—generative AI—and ﬁnd evidence that it most eﬀectively augments

lower-skill workers.

   For example, Peng et al. (2023b) recruit software engineers for a speciﬁc coding task (writing an

HTTP server in JavaScript) and show that those given access to GitHub Copilot complete this task

twice as quickly. Similarly, Noy and Zhang (2023) run an online experiment showing that subjects

given access to ChatGPT complete professional writing tasks more quickly. In addition, they show

that ChatGPT compresses the productivity distribution, with lower-skill workers beneﬁting the

most.

   To the best of our knowledge, however, there have been no studies of the impact of access to gen-

erative AI tools on productivity in real-world workplaces, nor over longer periods. Such studies are

important because the impact of AI on productivity may vary over time and interact with workers’

baseline level of experience or expertise. Technologies that look promising in laboratory settings

may have more limited eﬀects in practice because of the need for complementary organizational

investments, skill development and business process redesign. In addition, the introduction of AI

systems may have further impacts on worker and customer satisfaction, attrition, and patterns of

organizational behavior.


1  Generative AI and Large Language Models


In recent years, the rapid pace of AI development and public release tools such as ChatGPT,

GitHub Copilot, and DALL-E have attracted widespread attention, optimism, and alarm (The

White House, 2022). These technologies are all examples of “generative AI,” a class of machine



                                           3

learning technologies that can generate new content—such as text, images, music, or video—by

analyzing patterns in existing data. In this section, we provide background on generative AI as a

technology and discuss its potential economic implications.


1.1  Technical Primer

In this paper, we focus on an important class of generative AI, large language models (LLMs). At

a high level, LLMs are neural network models designed to process sequential data (Bubeck et al.,

2023).  For instance, an LLM can be trained by giving it access to a large corpus of text (such

as Wikipedia, digitized books, or portions of the Internet) and using that input text to learn to

predict the next word in a sequence, given what has come before. This knowledge of the statistical

co-occurrence of words allows it to generate new text that is grammatically correct and semantically

meaningful.

   Though the name implies human language, the same techniques can be used to produce LLMs

that generate other forms of sequential data such as protein sequences, audio, computer code, or

chess moves (Eloundou et al., 2023).

   Recent progress in generative AI has been driven by four factors: computing power, earlier

innovations in model architecture, the ability to “pre-train” using large amounts of unlabeled data,

and reﬁnements in training techniques.4  Model performance depends strongly on scale, which

includes the amount of computing power used for training, the number of model parameters, and

dataset size (Kaplan et al., 2020). Pre-training an LLM requires thousands of GPUs and weeks to

months of dedicated training time. For example, estimates indicate that a single training run for a

GPT-3 model with 175 billion parameters, trained on 300 billion tokens, may cost $5 million dollars

in just computing costs (Li, 2020; Brown et al., 2020).

   In terms of model architecture, modern LLMs make use of two earlier key innovations: positional

encoding and self-attention. Positional encodings keep track of the order in which a word occurs

in a given input.5 This allows large bodies of input text to be broken into smaller segments that

can be processed simultaneously without “forgetting” earlier parts of the input (Vaswani et al.,

2017; Bahdanau et al., 2015). Meanwhile, self-attention assigns importance weights to each word

in the context of the entire input text. Older approaches that assign importance based on word

frequencies that may misrepresent a word’s true semantic importance. These older methods may

also base on semantic content within a small window. In contrast, self-attention enables models to

   4For a more detailed technical review of progress, see Radford and Narasimhan (2018); Radford et al. (2019); Liu
et al. (2023); Ouyang et al. (2022).
   5For instance, a model would keep track of “the, 1” instead of only “the” (if “the” was the ﬁrst word in the sentence).




                                           4

capture long-range semantic relationships within an input text, even when that text is broken up

and processed in parallel (Vaswani et al., 2017).

   Second, LLMs can be pre-trained on large amounts of unlabeled data. For instance, GPT is

trained on unlabeled text data, allowing it to learn patterns in human language without explicit

guidance (Radford and Narasimhan, 2018).  Because unlabeled data is far more prevalent than

labeled data, this allows for LLMs to learn about natural language on a much larger training corpus

(Brown et al., 2020). The resulting model can be used in multiple applications because its training

is not speciﬁc to a particular set of tasks.6

    Finally, general-purpose LLMs can be further “ﬁne-tuned” to generate output that matches the

priorities of any speciﬁc setting (Ouyang et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2023). For example, an LLM may

generate several potential responses to a given query, but some of them may be factually incorrect

or biased. To discipline this model, human evaluators can rank these outputs to train a reward

function prioritizes some responses over others. Such reﬁnements can signiﬁcantly improve model

quality but making a general-purpose model better suited to its speciﬁc application (Ouyang et al.,

2022).

   Together, these innovations have generated meaningful improvements in model performance.

The Generative Pre-trained Transformer (GPT) family of models, in particular, has attracted con-

siderable media attention for their rapidly expanding capabilities.7


1.2  The Economic Impacts of Generative AI

Computers have historically excelled at executing pre-programmed instructions, making them par-

ticularly eﬀective at tasks that can be standardized and reduced to explicit rules (Autor, 2014).

Consequently, computerization has had a disproportionate impact on jobs that involve routine

tasks, such as data entry, bookkeeping, and assembly line work, and reducing demand for workers

performing “routine” tasks (Acemoglu and Autor, 2011). At the same time, computerization has

also increased the productivity of workers who possess complementary skills, such as programming,

data analysis, and research. Together, these changes have contributed to increasing wage inequality

in the United States and have been linked to a variety of organizational changes (Katz and Murphy,

1992; Autor et al., 2003; Michaels et al., 2014; Bresnahan et al., 2002; Baker and Hubbard, 2003).

   In contrast, recent advances in AI, particularly those driven by generative AI, suggest that it

is possible for LLMs to perform a variety of non-routine tasks such as software coding, persuasive

writing, and graphic design (Bommasani et al., 2021; Eloundou et al., 2023). For example, Copilot,

an AI pair programmer that generates code suggestions for programmers, has achieved impressive

performance on technical coding questions and generates an average of 46 percent of code among

users (Nguyen and Nadi, 2022; Zhao, 2023). Similarly, services like Elicit and Casetext use LLMs to

ﬁnd and summarize key information in legal documents or research, tasks that were previously con-

sidered non-routine (Elicit, 2023; Casetext, 2023). Since many of these tasks are currently performed

by workers who have either been insulated or beneﬁted from prior waves of technology adoption,

the expansion of generative AI has the potential to shift the relationship between technology, labor

productivity, and inequality (The White House, 2022).

   Unlike traditional programming, generative AI does not require explicit instructions as inputs.

Instead, it uses ML to mine vast amounts of human-generated data to recognize patterns, allowing

it to generate, summarize, and make inferences based on those patterns. For instance, if prompted

to provide a cover for a gothic novel, generative AI models will respond with an illustration that is

moody; if asked to write an email denying an employee a raise, generative AI will respond with a

note that is professional; this occurs even though no programmer has instructed the AI model as to

what tone would be appropriate in a given context. The ability to behave “appropriately” cannot

be reduced to a set of rules; instead people learn to do so from experience and apply unconscious

rules in the process. The fact that generative AI models display such skills suggests that they have

the potential to move past what has been termed “Polanyi’s Paradox,” the idea that knowledge is

diﬃcult to codify because individuals perform many tasks they cannot articulate (Polanyi, 1966;

Autor, 2014).

   At the same time, LLMs have signiﬁcant limitations. Popular LLM-based tools such as ChatGPT

have been shown to produce false or misleading information in unpredictable ways. While these

models often perform well on speciﬁc tasks in the lab, these concerns have raised questions about

their ability to perform well in more complex real-world settings (Peng et al., 2023a).


2  Our Setting: LLMs for Customer Support


2.1  Customer Support and Generative AI

We study the impact of generative AI in the customer service industry, an area with one the highest

surveyed rates of AI adoption.8 Customer support interactions are important for maintaining a

al., 2021).

company’s reputation and building strong customer relationships, yet as in many industries, there

is substantial variation in worker productivity (Berg et al., 2018; Syverson, 2011).

   Newer workers are also often less productive and require signiﬁcant training. At the same time,

turnover is high: industry estimates suggest that 60 percent of agents in contact centers9 leave each

year, costing ﬁrms $10,000 to $20,000 dollars per agent (Buesing et al., 2020; Gretz and Jacobson,

2018). To address these workforce challenges, the average supervisor spends at least 20 hours per

week coaching lower-performing agents (Berg et al., 2018). Faced with variable productivity, high

turnover, and high training costs, ﬁrms are increasingly turning toward AI tools (Chui et al., 2021).

   At a technical level, customer support is well-suited for current generative AI tools. From an

AI’s perspective, customer-agent conversations can be thought of as a series of pattern-matching

problems in which one is looking for an optimal sequence of actions. When confronted with an issue

such as “I can’t login,” an AI/agent must identify which types of underlying problems are most likely

to lead a customer to be unable to log in and think about which solutions typically resolve these

problems (“Can you check that caps lock is not on?”). At the same time, they must be attuned to

a customer’s emotional response, making sure to use language that increases the likelihood that a

customer will respond positively (“that wasn’t stupid of you at all!  I always forget to check that

too!”). Because customer service conversations are widely recorded and digitized, pre-trained LLMs

can be ﬁne-tuned for customer service using many examples of both successfully and unsuccessfully

resolved conversations.

   In the remainder of this section, we provide details about the ﬁrm we study and the AI tool

they adopt.


2.2  Data Firm Background

We work with a company that provides AI-based customer service support software (hereafter, the

“AI ﬁrm”) to study the deployment of their tool at one of their client ﬁrms, (hereafter, the “data

ﬁrm”).

   Our data ﬁrm is a Fortune 500 enterprise software company that specializes in business process

software for small and medium-sized businesses in the United States.   It employs a variety of

chat-based technical support agents, both directly and through third-party ﬁrms. The majority of

agents in our sample work from oﬃces located in the Philippines, with a smaller group working in

the United States and in other countries. Across locations, agents are engaged in a fairly uniform

2.3  AI System Design

The AI system we study uses a generative model system that combines a recent version of GPT

with additional ML algorithms speciﬁcally ﬁne-tuned to focus on customer service interactions. The

system is further trained on a large set of customer-agent conversations that have been labeled with

a variety of outcomes and characteristics: whether the call was successfully resolved, how long it

took to handle the call, and whether the agent in charge of the call is considered a “top” performer

by the data ﬁrm. The AI ﬁrm then uses these data to look for conversational patterns that are

most predictive of call resolution and handle time.

   The AI ﬁrm further trains its model using a process similar in spirit to Ouyang et al. (2022) to

prioritize agent responses that express empathy, surface appropriate technical documentation, and

limit unprofessional language. This additional training mitigates some of concerns associated with

relying on LLMs to generate text.

   Once deployed, the AI system generates two main types of outputs: 1) real-time suggestions for

how agents should respond to customers and 2) links to the data ﬁrm’s internal documentation for

relevant technical issues. In both cases, recommendations are based on a history of the conversation.

For example, the correct response when a customer says “I can’t track my employee’s hours during

need to diagnose and resolve a technical issue preventing the software from working.  If, however,

the customer stated that they are using the standard version, then the correct solution is for the

customer to upgrade to the premium version in order to access this feature.10

The output is shown only to the agent, who has full discretion over whether to incorporate (fully or

partially) the AI suggestions. This reduces the potential for output that is oﬀ-topic or incorrect to

4.5  Textual Evidence

Our evidence so far suggests that access to AI suggestions improves productivity and, for the lower-

skilled and less-experienced agents, increases conversation quality as measured by resolution rates

and surveyed customer satisfaction.

   Next, we consider why AI may have these impacts. This section provides evidence from prelim-

inary analysis of the textual content of chat conversations. Our goal is to understand whether and

how AI recommendations change the way agents communicate.

   In particular, we are interested in AI model’s ability to encode the potentially tacit knowledge of

high performers: does AI assistance lead lower-skill workers to communicate more like higher-skill

workers? Because tacit knowledge is, by deﬁnition, not something that can be codiﬁed as a set of

rules, we examine the overall textual similarity of conversations rather than looking for the presence

of speciﬁc formulaic phrases.

  We begin by constructing textual embeddings of agent-customer conversations. These embed-

dings allow us to represent their semantic and stylistic content as a vector so that we can compare

one conversation to another using cosine similarity. Cosine similarity is a widely-used metric for

measuring the similarity of two embeddings.  It calculates the cosine of the angle between two n-

dimensional vectors, where values close to 1 indicate similarity (Koroteev, 2021). We form our text

embeddings using all-MiniLM-L6-v2, an LLM that is speciﬁcally intended to capture and cluster

semantic information in order to assess similarity (Hugging Face, 2023). We then compare how an

agent’s conversations change over time (e.g. within-person similarity over time), as well as how high-

and low-skill agents’ conversations compare with each other over time (between-person similarity

at a given point in time).


4.5.1  Within-worker changes in communication

To examine how AI changes agent conversations with customers, we begin by comparing an individ-

ual agent’s text pre- and post-AI model deployment. We take a given agent’s corpus of text from

an eight-week window before deployment and compare it with text from the same-sized window af-

terward. We exclude the three weeks around deployment to account for disruptions due to training

and individual adjustment to the AI model. We exclude messages from the customer, and focus

only on agent-generated language. Then, for each individual agent, we plot textual dissimilarity be-

tween pre- and post-AI conversations as one minus the cosine similarity. The within-person textual

diﬀerence in our data is roughly 0.3, indicating that, on average, agents continue to communicate

similarly after the deployment of the AI model. For context, the sentences “Can you help me with

this logging in?” and “Why is my login not working?” have a cosine similarity of 0.68.

  We examine how language changes pre- and post-AI for workers who are initially high- and low-

skill, where high-skill workers are deﬁned as those in the top quintile of the skill index distribution,

while low-skill workers are those in the bottom quintile.

     If the AI is able to embody and disseminate some of the tacit “best practices” of high-skill

workers, then we would expect low-skill workers to experience a greater shift in communication

patterns following access to AI assistance (high-skill workers would change less since the AI model is

suggesting practices they have already adopted). In Panel A of Figure 12, we ﬁnd evidence consistent

with this hypothesis: initially lower-skill agents shift their language more after AI model deployment,

relative to initially higher-skill workers. The scores we plot include controls for conversation timing

to account for seasonal changes in topics such as tax season or payroll cycles. These results also

control for agent tenure to account for the possibility that younger workers’ language may evolve

more quickly independent of access to the AI model.

     If AI assistance merely leads workers to type the same things but faster, then we would not

expect this diﬀerential change. And because chats are randomly allocated to agents, we would not

also expect the pattern we document to be driven by diﬀerential changes in conversation topics

between high and low-skill workers.


4.5.2  Across worker comparisons

We next explore how lower-skill agents’ language choices change with AI assistance. In Panel B of

more like high-skill agents. In particular, we plot the cosine similarity between high- and low-skill

agents at speciﬁc moments in calendar time, separately for workers with (blue dots) and without

(red diamonds) access to AI assistance. Among agents without access, we deﬁne high- and low-skill

agents as those who are in the top or bottom quintile of our skill index for that month. Among

agents with access, we deﬁne high- and low-skill agents based on whether they are in the top or

bottom quintile of skill at the time of deployment.

productivity workers is 0.55. This ﬁgure is lower than our average within-person text similarity

(0.73), which makes sense given that these are across-person comparisons.  Textual similarity is

stable over time, suggesting that high- and low-skill workers are not trending diﬀerently in the

4.6  Eﬀects on the Experience and Organization of Work

Access to AI assistance may impact workers and the ﬁrm organization as a whole through changes in

work experience, turnover, and task allocation. In this section, we examine some of these outcomes.


4.6.1  Sentiment

Customers often vent their frustrations on anonymous service agents and, in our data, we see regular

instances of swearing, verbal abuse, and “yelling” (typing in all caps). A key part of agents’ jobs is

to absorb customer frustrations while restraining one’s own emotional reaction (Hochschild, 2019).

The stress associated with this type of emotional labor is often cited as a key cause of burnout and

attrition among customer service workers (Lee, 2015). It is unclear what impact AI assistants may

have on the tenor of conversations: AI recommendations may help the agent more eﬀectively set the

customer’s expectations or resolve their problem, but customers may react poorly if AI-suggested

language feels “corporate” or insincere.

   To assess this, we attempt to capture the aﬀective nature of both agent and customer text, using

sentiment analysis (Mejova, 2009). For this analysis, we use SiEBERT, an LLM that is ﬁne-tuned

for sentiment analysis using a variety of datasets, including product reviews and tweets (Hartmann

et al., 2023). Sentiment is measured on a scale from ´1 to 1. We compute sentiment scores for

the agent and customer text of each chat separately, and then aggregate across all chats for each

agent-year-month.

   Panels A and B of Figure 13 describe the distributions of average customer and visitor sentiment

scores. On average, customer sentiments in our data are mildly positive and normally distributed

around a mean of 0.14 except for a mass of very positive and very negative scores. As one might

expect, customer service agents are trained to be extremely positive and professional so agent

sentiment scores are almost always highly positive, with a mean of 0.89.

   Panels C and D consider how sentiment scores respond to the introduction of the AI assistant.

In Panel C, we see an immediate and persistent improvement in customer sentiment. This eﬀect is

sentiments (averaged over an agent-month) by 0.18 points, equivalent to half of a standard deviation.

We see a much smaller impact on agent scores. In Panel D, we see no detectable eﬀect for agent

sentiment, which unsurprising because agent’s expressed sentiment is already very high. Column 2

of Table 4 indicates that agent sentiments increase by only 0.02 points or about one percent of a

Consistent with our main results, we ﬁnd that most sentiment improvements occur for workers with

We ﬁnd the largest eﬀects for workers with 3-6 months of tenure at AI model deployment, and we

suggest that AI recommendations, which were explicitly designed to prioritize more empathetic

responses, may improve agents’ social skills and have a positive emotional impact on customers.


4.6.2  Attrition

Increases in worker-level productivity do not always lead workers to be happier with their jobs.  If

workers become more productive but dislike being managed by an AI assistant, this may lead to

greater turnover.  If, on the other hand, AI assistance reduces stress, then workers may be more

likely to stay.

   Here, we examine how the deployment of the AI tool impacts worker attrition. For this analysis,

we compare agents who are never treated with treated agents after treatment. In particular, we drop

observations for treated agents prior to treatment because this group experiences no attrition in

this period by construction (they must survive to be treated in the future). Our analysis compares

the trajectories of agents with the same tenure but diﬀerent access to AI assistance, controlling for

location and time ﬁxed eﬀects.

on average, the likelihood that a worker leaves in the current month goes down by 8.6 percentage

points. Figure 14 considers how these patterns depend on an agent’s tenure or skill at the time the AI

system is introduced. We ﬁnd the strongest reductions in attrition among newer agents, those with

less than 6 months of experience. The magnitude of this coeﬃcient, around 10 percentage points,

eﬀect may be overstated if access to the AI tool is more likely to be given to agents whom the ﬁrm

deems more likely to stay. Without agent-ﬁxed eﬀects in our speciﬁcation, we cannot account for

4.6.3  Vertical and Horizontal Workﬂow

Changes in individual worker-level productivity may have broader implications for organizational

workﬂows (Garicano, 2000; Athey et al., 1994; Athey and Stern, 1998). In most ﬁrms, customer

support agents are organized both vertically and horizontally.  Vertically, front-line agents try to

resolve customer problems but can seek the help of supervisors when they are unsure of how to

proceed. Customers in our data will sometimes attempt to escalate a conversation by asking to

speak to a manager.  This type of request generally occurs when the customer feels the current

agent is not equipped to address their problem or becomes frustrated. Our data ﬁrm, like most

other contact centers, employs designated “escalation agents” to deal with these requests.

    Horizontally, agents often represent speciﬁc departments that handle speciﬁc tasks. For example,

some may specialize in technical software issues while others specialize in account management

issues. A customer with a technical issue requiring that their account be upgraded to a premium

product would likely be transferred to a diﬀerent department.

   In Figure 15 and Table 5, we consider the impact of AI model deployment on vertical and

horizontal assistance. We do not have a direct measure of whether a call is actually escalated to the

manager. Instead, we examine chat-level text data to examine requests for escalations: instances

in which a customer requests to speak to a manager or supervisor. In Column 1 of Table 5, we

ﬁnd that AI assistance generates an almost 25 percent decline in customer requests to speak to a

manager. The accompanying event study is presented in Panel A of Figure 15: we see that declines

in requests are persistent and grow over time.

of horizontal transfers to other agents.  In Column 2 of Table 5, we see a positively-signed but

statistically insigniﬁcant impact on transfers. Panel B of Figure 15 suggests that transfers initially

increase but then slowly decline. Upon reviewing the text of these conversations, we see that most

transfers appear to redirect customers to a more appropriate department. Many of these transfers

occur early in the call, suggesting that transfers reﬂect a matching between a customer’s problem

and an agent’s specialty.

5  Conclusion


Progress in machine learning opens up a broad set of economic possibilities. Our paper provides

the ﬁrst empirical evidence on the eﬀects of a generative AI tool in a real-world workplace.  In

our setting, we ﬁnd that access to AI-generated recommendations increases worker productivity,

improves customer sentiment, and is associated with reductions in employee turnover.

  We hypothesize the part of the eﬀect we document is driven by the AI system’s ability to

embody the best practices of high-skill workers in our ﬁrm. These practices may have previously

been diﬃcult to disseminate because they involve tacit knowledge. Consistent with this, we see that

AI assistance leads to substantial improvements in problem resolution and customer satisfaction for

newer- and less-skilled workers, but does not help the highest-skilled or most-experienced workers

on these measures. Analyzing the text of agent conversations, we ﬁnd suggestive evidence that AI

recommendations lead low-skill workers to communicate more like high-skill workers.

   Our ﬁndings, and their limitations, point to a variety of directions for future research.

   As a potential general-purpose technology, generative AI can and will be deployed in a variety of

ways, and the eﬀects we ﬁnd may not generalize across all ﬁrms and production processes (Eloundou

et al., 2023). For example, our setting has a relatively stable product and set of technical support

questions. In areas where the product or environment is changing rapidly, the relative value of AI

recommendations—trained on historical data—may be diﬀerent.

   Our results do not capture potential longer-term impacts on skill demand, job design, wages, or

customer demand. For example, more eﬀective technical support could accelerate the trend towards

contact center agents taking on more complex customer responsibilities, increasing aggregate de-

mand even if agents become more productive (Berg et al., 2018; Korinek, 2022). And over the longer

term, these tools can uncover patterns and insights that may not be documented in formal channels,

changing the way workers are managed or how knowledge is shared within an organization.

    Finally, our ﬁndings raise questions about whether and how workers should be compensated for

the data that they provide to AI systems. High-skill workers, in particular, play an important role

in model development but see smaller direct beneﬁts in terms of improving their own productivity.

   Given the early stage of generative AI, these and other questions deserve further scrutiny.

S006.quote:
We study the staggered introduction of a generative AI-based conversational assistant using
data from 5,179 customer support agents. Access to the tool increases productivity, as measured
by issues resolved per hour, by 14 percent on average, with the greatest impact on novice and
low-skilled workers, and minimal impact on experienced and highly skilled workers. We provide
suggestive evidence that the AI model disseminates the potentially tacit knowledge of more able
workers and helps newer workers move down the experience curve. In addition, we show that
AI assistance improves customer sentiment, reduces requests for managerial intervention, and
improves employee retention.

Generative AI and Large Language Models

S102.quote: In recent years, the rapid pace of AI development and public release tools such as ChatGPT,

S103.quote: GitHub Copilot, and DALL-E have attracted widespread attention, optimism, and alarm (The

S104.quote: White House, 2022). These technologies are all examples of “generative AI,” a class of machine

S105.quote: learning technologies that can generate new content—such as text, images, music, or video—by

S106.quote: analyzing patterns in existing data. In this section, we provide background on generative AI as a

S107.quote: technology and discuss its potential economic implications.

S109.quote: In this paper, we focus on an important class of generative AI, large language models (LLMs). At

S110.quote: a high level, LLMs are neural network models designed to process sequential data (Bubeck et al.,

S111.quote: 2023). For instance, an LLM can be trained by giving it access to a large corpus of text (such

S112.quote: as Wikipedia, digitized books, or portions of the Internet) and using that input text to learn to

S113.quote: predict the next word in a sequence, given what has come before. This knowledge of the statistical

S114.quote: co-occurrence of words allows it to generate new text that is grammatically correct and semantically

S116.quote: Though the name implies human language, the same techniques can be used to produce LLMs

S117.quote: that generate other forms of sequential data such as protein sequences, audio, computer code, or

S119.quote: Recent progress in generative AI has been driven by four factors: computing power, earlier

S120.quote: innovations in model architecture, the ability to “pre-train” using large amounts of unlabeled data,

S121.quote:
and reﬁnements in training techniques.4
Model performance depends strongly on scale, which

S122.quote: includes the amount of computing power used for training, the number of model parameters, and

S123.quote: dataset size (Kaplan et al., 2020). Pre-training an LLM requires thousands of GPUs and weeks to

S124.quote: months of dedicated training time. For example, estimates indicate that a single training run for a

S125.quote: GPT-3 model with 175 billion parameters, trained on 300 billion tokens, may cost $5 million dollars

S126.quote: in just computing costs (Li, 2020; Brown et al., 2020).

S127.quote: In terms of model architecture, modern LLMs make use of two earlier key innovations: positional

S128.quote: encoding and self-attention. Positional encodings keep track of the order in which a word occurs

S129.quote: in a given input.5 This allows large bodies of input text to be broken into smaller segments that

S130.quote: can be processed simultaneously without “forgetting” earlier parts of the input (Vaswani et al.,

S131.quote: 2017; Bahdanau et al., 2015). Meanwhile, self-attention assigns importance weights to each word

S132.quote: in the context of the entire input text. Older approaches that assign importance based on word

S133.quote: frequencies that may misrepresent a word’s true semantic importance. These older methods may

S134.quote: also base on semantic content within a small window. In contrast, self-attention enables models to

S137.quote: capture long-range semantic relationships within an input text, even when that text is broken up

S138.quote: and processed in parallel (Vaswani et al., 2017).

S139.quote: Second, LLMs can be pre-trained on large amounts of unlabeled data. For instance, GPT is

S140.quote: trained on unlabeled text data, allowing it to learn patterns in human language without explicit

S141.quote:
guidance (Radford and Narasimhan, 2018).
Because unlabeled data is far more prevalent than

S142.quote: labeled data, this allows for LLMs to learn about natural language on a much larger training corpus

S143.quote: (Brown et al., 2020). The resulting model can be used in multiple applications because its training

S144.quote: is not speciﬁc to a particular set of tasks.6

S146.quote: priorities of any speciﬁc setting (Ouyang et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2023). For example, an LLM may

S152.quote: The Generative Pre-trained Transformer (GPT) family of models, in particular, has attracted con-

S153.quote: siderable media attention for their rapidly expanding capabilities.7

The Economic Impacts of Generative AI

S155.quote: Computers have historically excelled at executing pre-programmed instructions, making them par-

S156.quote: ticularly eﬀective at tasks that can be standardized and reduced to explicit rules (Autor, 2014).

S157.quote: Consequently, computerization has had a disproportionate impact on jobs that involve routine

S158.quote: tasks, such as data entry, bookkeeping, and assembly line work, and reducing demand for workers

S159.quote: performing “routine” tasks (Acemoglu and Autor, 2011). At the same time, computerization has

S160.quote: also increased the productivity of workers who possess complementary skills, such as programming,

S161.quote: data analysis, and research. Together, these changes have contributed to increasing wage inequality

S162.quote: in the United States and have been linked to a variety of organizational changes (Katz and Murphy,

S163.quote: 1992; Autor et al., 2003; Michaels et al., 2014; Bresnahan et al., 2002; Baker and Hubbard, 2003).

S164.quote: In contrast, recent advances in AI, particularly those driven by generative AI, suggest that it

S165.quote: is possible for LLMs to perform a variety of non-routine tasks such as software coding, persuasive

S200.quote: Newer workers are also often less productive and require signiﬁcant training. At the same time,

S201.quote: turnover is high: industry estimates suggest that 60 percent of agents in contact centers9 leave each

S215.quote: can be ﬁne-tuned for customer service using many examples of both successfully and unsuccessfully

S247.quote: The AI system we study uses a generative model system that combines a recent version of GPT

S248.quote: with additional ML algorithms speciﬁcally ﬁne-tuned to focus on customer service interactions. The

S249.quote: system is further trained on a large set of customer-agent conversations that have been labeled with

S251.quote: took to handle the call, and whether the agent in charge of the call is considered a “top” performer

S252.quote: by the data ﬁrm. The AI ﬁrm then uses these data to look for conversational patterns that are

S253.quote: most predictive of call resolution and handle time.

S529.quote: We begin by constructing textual embeddings of agent-customer conversations. These embed-

S530.quote: dings allow us to represent their semantic and stylistic content as a vector so that we can compare

S531.quote: one conversation to another using cosine similarity. Cosine similarity is a widely-used metric for

S532.quote: measuring the similarity of two embeddings. It calculates the cosine of the angle between two n-

S533.quote: dimensional vectors, where values close to 1 indicate similarity (Koroteev, 2021). We form our text

S534.quote: embeddings using all-MiniLM-L6-v2, an LLM that is speciﬁcally intended to capture and cluster

S535.quote: semantic information in order to assess similarity (Hugging Face, 2023). We then compare how an

S679.quote: Progress in machine learning opens up a broad set of economic possibilities. Our paper provides

S680.quote: the ﬁrst empirical evidence on the eﬀects of a generative AI tool in a real-world workplace. In

S681.quote: our setting, we ﬁnd that access to AI-generated recommendations increases worker productivity,

S682.quote: improves customer sentiment, and is associated with reductions in employee turnover.

S683.quote: We hypothesize the part of the eﬀect we document is driven by the AI system’s ability to

S684.quote: embody the best practices of high-skill workers in our ﬁrm. These practices may have previously

S685.quote: been diﬃcult to disseminate because they involve tacit knowledge. Consistent with this, we see that

S686.quote: AI assistance leads to substantial improvements in problem resolution and customer satisfaction for

S687.quote: newer- and less-skilled workers, but does not help the highest-skilled or most-experienced workers

S688.quote: on these measures. Analyzing the text of agent conversations, we ﬁnd suggestive evidence that AI

S689.quote: recommendations lead low-skill workers to communicate more like high-skill workers.

S690.quote: Our ﬁndings, and their limitations, point to a variety of directions for future research.

S691.quote: As a potential general-purpose technology, generative AI can and will be deployed in a variety of

S692.quote: ways, and the eﬀects we ﬁnd may not generalize across all ﬁrms and production processes (Eloundou

S693.quote: et al., 2023). For example, our setting has a relatively stable product and set of technical support

S694.quote: questions. In areas where the product or environment is changing rapidly, the relative value of AI

S695.quote: recommendations—trained on historical data—may be diﬀerent.

S696.quote: Our results do not capture potential longer-term impacts on skill demand, job design, wages, or

S697.quote: customer demand. For example, more eﬀective technical support could accelerate the trend towards

S698.quote: contact center agents taking on more complex customer responsibilities, increasing aggregate de-

S699.quote: mand even if agents become more productive (Berg et al., 2018; Korinek, 2022). And over the longer

S700.quote: term, these tools can uncover patterns and insights that may not be documented in formal channels,

S701.quote: changing the way workers are managed or how knowledge is shared within an organization.

S702.quote: Finally, our ﬁndings raise questions about whether and how workers should be compensated for

S703.quote: the data that they provide to AI systems. High-skill workers, in particular, play an important role

S704.quote: in model development but see smaller direct beneﬁts in terms of improving their own productivity.

S705.quote: Given the early stage of generative AI, these and other questions deserve further scrutiny.

concept-0a234433145240a9.title: 生成式 AI (Generative AI)
concept-0a234433145240a9.lead: 能够生成新内容（如文本、图像）的 AI 系统。
concept-0a234433145240a9.text: 在本文中，生成式 AI 指基于大型语言模型（LLM）的工具，能够分析现有数据中的模式并生成新的响应内容。它与传统编程不同，不需要显式的指令编码，而是从示例中学习。
concept-0a234433145240a9.why: 理解该概念是区分本研究与以往自动化研究的基础，因为生成式 AI 能处理非结构化任务和隐性知识。

concept-9166bf36d4e11321.title: 隐性知识 (Tacit Knowledge)
concept-9166bf36d4e11321.lead: 难以通过语言或文字明确表达的知识，通常通过经验获得。
concept-9166bf36d4e11321.text: 指那些无法轻易编码或指令化的生产过程中的知识。作者假设 AI 系统能够捕捉高技能工人的隐性知识（通过其行为模式），并将其传播给低技能工人，从而缩小技能差距。
concept-9166bf36d4e11321.why: 这是解释为何 AI 主要帮助低技能工人的核心机制假设。

concept-be42c7c54b9d8aaa.title: 微调 (Fine-tuning)
concept-be42c7c54b9d8aaa.lead: 在预训练模型基础上使用特定领域数据进行的额外训练。
concept-be42c7c54b9d8aaa.text: 本研究中，基础 GPT 模型使用了特定的客户 - 代理对话数据进行微调，这些数据标记了解决状态和代理绩效。这使得模型能够学习特定于该技术支持环境的最佳实践，而不仅仅是通用语言模式。
concept-be42c7c54b9d8aaa.why: 解释了为何通用 LLM 能在此特定工作场景中产生高价值建议。

concept-093adf1f9e08a97e.title: 基于人类反馈的优化 (类似 RLHF 的过程)
concept-093adf1f9e08a97e.lead: 调整模型输出以符合人类价值观和特定目标的技术。
concept-093adf1f9e08a97e.text: 文中提到系统经过进一步训练，以优先选择表达同理心、提供准确文档链接并限制不专业语言的回复。这种训练减轻了直接使用 LLM 生成文本的一些担忧（如幻觉或不恰当内容）。
concept-093adf1f9e08a97e.why: 说明了系统如何保证建议的质量和安全性，使其适合企业环境。

concept-87ad284076372608.title: 交错部署 (Staggered Deployment)
concept-87ad284076372608.lead: 处理组在不同时间点陆续接受干预的实验设计。
concept-87ad284076372608.text: 在本研究中，AI 工具不是同时分配给所有代理，而是在一段时间内逐步 rollout。这种设计允许研究者比较同一代理在接收工具前后的表现，以及不同时间接收工具的队列之间的差异，从而构建反事实。
concept-87ad284076372608.why: 这是识别因果效应的关键数据来源，使得双重差分方法可行。

concept-8685206aa781a70e.title: Sun & Abraham (2021) 估计量
concept-8685206aa781a70e.lead: 一种用于处理交错采用双重差分中异质性处理效应的稳健估计方法。
concept-8685206aa781a70e.text: 当处理效应随时间变化或在不同采用队列间存在差异时，传统的双重差分估计量可能不一致。Sun & Abraham (2021) 提出的交互加权估计量通过聚合队列特定的事件时间效应来解决这一问题，前提是满足平行趋势假设。
concept-8685206aa781a70e.why: 该方法确保了在处理效应动态变化复杂的情况下，研究结论的统计可靠性。

concept-07ed60823dc56197.title: 每小时解决量 (Resolutions Per Hour)
concept-07ed60823dc56197.lead: 衡量客服生产力的主要因变量。
concept-07ed60823dc56197.text: 指代理在一小时内成功解决的技术支持问题数量。该指标综合反映了处理速度和多任务处理能力。
concept-07ed60823dc56197.why: 这是本文评估 AI 影响的最关键产出指标，直接对应劳动力经济学中的生产率定义。

concept-beb2726e9b0e94be.title: 意向治疗效应 (Intent-to-Treat)
concept-beb2726e9b0e94be.lead: 本文主要报告的估计策略。
concept-beb2726e9b0e94be.text: 指评估“获得 AI 访问权限”这一事件本身的影响，无论代理实际使用或遵循 AI 建议的频率如何。这避免了因代理选择性使用工具而产生的内生性偏差。
concept-beb2726e9b0e94be.why: 理解此概念有助于明白为何文中数据反映的是‘接入’带来的平均效果，而非‘完美使用’下的理论上限。

concept-ab847cf8a03a7f06.title: 技能五分位 (Skill Quintiles)
concept-ab847cf8a03a7f06.lead: 用于分析异质性效应的代理分类标准。
concept-ab847cf8a03a7f06.text: 作者根据代理在 AI 部署前一个季度的三个关键指标（平均处理时长、解决率、客户满意度）计算综合技能指数，并在每个公司 - 月份内将代理分为五组。Q1 代表技能最低的 20%，Q5 代表技能最高的 20%。
concept-ab847cf8a03a7f06.why: 这种动态分组确保了比较是在同等相对水平的代理之间进行，排除了公司间固有差异的干扰，是识别‘技能偏向型’技术变革的关键设计。

concept-50a77f6bb0e6795c.title: 经验曲线 (Experience Curve)
concept-50a77f6bb0e6795c.lead: 描述绩效随工作时间积累的演变路径。
concept-50a77f6bb0e6795c.text: 在本文中，指代理的生产力（每小时解决量）随其在公司任职月数增加而变化的轨迹。传统上，这是一条平缓上升的曲线，代表‘熟能生巧’的过程。AI 的作用是使这条曲线变得更陡峭，缩短了达到熟练水平所需的时间。
concept-50a77f6bb0e6795c.why: 这是理解 AI 如何替代或加速人力资本积累的核心概念。它解释了为何 AI 对新手价值最大——因为它压缩了新手最需要漫长的‘试错学习’阶段。

concept-a9e5ecf658d9f02e.title: 余弦相似度 (Cosine Similarity)
concept-a9e5ecf658d9f02e.lead: 衡量两个向量在多维空间中方向一致性的指标。
concept-a9e5ecf658d9f02e.text: 在本文本分析中，余弦相似度用于量化两段对话文本在语义和风格上的接近程度。值为 1 表示完全相同，0 表示正交（无相关性）。研究者用它来比较不同技能水平员工的语言向量。
concept-a9e5ecf658d9f02e.why: 理解该指标是解读“语言趋同”结论的基础，它证明了变化不仅是词汇的重复，而是整体沟通风格的靠近。

concept-96e15d3b33b7edc8.title: 隐性知识 (Tacit Knowledge)
concept-96e15d3b33b7edc8.lead: 难以通过书面规则或公式明确表达的知识，通常通过经验获得。
concept-96e15d3b33b7edc8.text: 在客户服务中，隐性知识包括如何安抚愤怒客户、何时使用幽默或非正式语气等微妙技巧。文章假设 AI 模型通过学习高绩效者的数据，将这些难以编码的经验转化为具体的建议，从而传递给低技能员工。
concept-96e15d3b33b7edc8.why: 这是解释为何低技能员工能迅速提升表现且语言风格发生改变的核心理论机制。

concept-0818efd0311e1d8d.title: 情感分析 (Sentiment Analysis)
concept-0818efd0311e1d8d.lead: 利用自然语言处理技术识别文本中的情绪倾向（如积极、消极）。
concept-0818efd0311e1d8d.text: 本研究使用 SiEBERT 模型，该模型经过产品评论和推文等多种数据集的微调，能够评分从 -1 到 1 的情感值。研究者分别计算客服人员和客户的情感得分，以评估 AI 对互动质量的影响。
concept-0818efd0311e1d8d.why: 这是量化“客户满意度”和“员工情绪劳动”的关键技术手段，解释了为何 AI 能改善软性指标。

concept-cc8004fca5617322.title: 流失率 (Attrition)
concept-cc8004fca5617322.lead: 指员工离开组织的比率，是衡量工作满意度和组织健康的重要指标。
concept-cc8004fca5617322.text: 在客服中心，高流失率通常与高压、低胜任感和情绪耗竭有关。文章发现 AI 辅助显著降低了新员工的流失率，暗示工具可能通过降低认知负荷或提供即时支持，缓解了新手常见的挫败感。
concept-cc8004fca5617322.why: 连接了技术干预与人力资源成本，展示了 AI 在经济效率之外的管理价值。

concept-37aa089890367534.title: 意向治疗分析 (Intent-to-Treat, ITT)
concept-37aa089890367534.lead: 一种分析方法，按初始分配的组别（如是否获得 AI 权限）评估效果，无论受试者实际执行情况如何。
concept-37aa089890367534.text: 文章主要报告的是 ITT 效应，即只要员工获得了 AI 访问权，无论他们是否真的使用了建议，都计入处理组。这反映了政策实施的真实效果。随后，作者专门分析了“依从性”以探讨实际使用程度与回报的关系。
concept-37aa089890367534.why: 区分 ITT 和依从性分析对于理解 AI 的实际潜力和政策落地效果至关重要。ITT 显示了“提供工具”的价值，而依从性分析揭示了“使用工具”的边际收益。

concept-4d80cd2e2047a138.title: 基于收益的选择 (Selection on Gains)
concept-4d80cd2e2047a138.lead: 一种偏差来源，指那些能从干预中获得最大收益的人最有可能去执行该干预。
concept-4d80cd2e2047a138.text: 在解释依从度与生产力的正相关时，作者提出这可能不仅是“听从建议导致高效”，也可能是“那些最能从 AI 中获益的员工更倾向于听从建议”。这种内生性使得因果推断变得复杂。
concept-4d80cd2e2047a138.why: 提醒读者注意观察到的强相关性（高依从=高产出）不一定完全是因果关系，可能存在自我选择机制。

concept-14f45bc0417008c2.title: 隐性知识转移 (Tacit Knowledge Transfer)
concept-14f45bc0417008c2.lead: 指难以通过书面文档形式化，需通过观察或实践传递的专业技能。
concept-14f45bc0417008c2.text: 在本文中，生成式 AI 被假设能够体现高技能员工的最佳实践，这些实践通常包含隐性知识，此前难以传播（pdf-ac0a4e183aa6f936-p23-b8, pdf-ac0a4e183aa6f936-p23-b9）。AI 通过将这些隐性模式转化为显性推荐，帮助低技能员工模仿高技能员工的沟通方式（pdf-ac0a4e183aa6f936-p23-b13）。
concept-14f45bc0417008c2.why: 理解此概念是解释为何 AI 能显著提升低技能员工表现，而对高技能员工影响有限的核心机制。

concept-2f38b5201c5608cf.title: 通用技术情境依赖性 (GPT Context Dependency)
concept-2f38b5201c5608cf.lead: 通用技术（如电力、AI）虽应用广泛，但其具体经济效应高度依赖于部署环境和互补性投资。
concept-2f38b5201c5608cf.text: 作者指出生成式 AI 是一种潜在的通用技术，但其在不同公司和生产流程中的效果可能不同（pdf-ac0a4e183aa6f936-p23-b15, pdf-ac0a4e183aa6f936-p23-b16）。特别是在环境快速变化时，基于历史数据的模型价值会受限，这表明技术效果并非普遍恒定，而是依赖于具体的组织情境和互补性流程（pdf-ac0a4e183aa6f936-p4-b24, pdf-ac0a4e183aa6f936-p23-b19）。
concept-2f38b5201c5608cf.why: 此概念解释了为何不能将本研究的特定结果简单外推至所有行业，强调了环境稳定性作为关键边界条件的重要性。
